## Prepare geographic and income information
The HRSA crosswalk assigns postal ZIP codes to Census ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs). The Census table supplies median household income and its margin of error for each ZCTA. We prepare one row per ZIP, retaining the area identifier so the source of each income estimate stays visible.

## Load the packages
```{r}
#| label: income-preparation-setup
library(tidyverse)
```

## Read the ZIP-to-area crosswalk
Read the saved workbook as text to preserve identifier formatting, including leading zeros. Give ZIP its working name, `zipcode`, here.
```{r}
#| label: read-zip-crosswalk
zip_crosswalk <- readxl::read_excel(
  "data/raw/ZIPCodetoZCTACrosswalk2024UDS.xlsx",
  sheet = "ZiptoZCTA",
  col_types = "text"
) |>
  rename(
    zipcode = ZIP_CODE,
    post_office = PO_NAME,
    state = STATE,
    zcta = ZCTA,
    zip_join_type = ZIP_JOIN_TYPE
  )
```

## Mark the ZIPs selected by our NYC rule
The prefix lookup assigns boroughs; 11004 and 11005 are included separately as Queens. This is our existing selection rule, not an exact geographic boundary test. `str_sub()` takes the first three characters. The left join keeps every crosswalk row, including prefixes without a borough. `in_nyc` records the classification without removing rows.
```{r}
#| label: flag-nyc-zips
nyc_prefixes <- tribble(
  ~zip_prefix, ~borough,
  "100", "Manhattan",
  "101", "Manhattan",
  "102", "Manhattan",
  "103", "Staten Island",
  "104", "Bronx",
  "111", "Queens",
  "112", "Brooklyn",
  "113", "Queens",
  "114", "Queens",
  "116", "Queens"
)

zip_crosswalk |>
  mutate(zip_prefix = str_sub(zipcode, 1, 3)) |>                # characters 1 to 3
  left_join(nyc_prefixes, by = "zip_prefix") |>
  mutate(borough = case_when(
    zipcode == "11004" | zipcode == "11005" ~ "Queens",           # Glen Oaks, Floral Park
    .default = borough
  )) |>
  mutate(in_nyc = !is.na(borough)) ->
  zip_areas
```

## Read the saved Census income table
The JSON file contains a grid of text, with headings in its first row. Assign those headings, remove that first row, and turn the remaining records into a tibble. The empty position after the comma means all columns.
```{r}
#| label: read-saved-census-income
income_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON("data/raw/acs5_2024_b19013_zcta.json")
colnames(income_raw) <- income_raw[1, ]

income_raw[-1, ] |>
  as_tibble() ->
  income_records
```

## Select the supplied area identifier and amounts
The Census supplies the ZCTA identifier directly. Keep it as text and retain the two amounts needed for preparation.
```{r}
#| label: select-income-fields
income_records |>
  rename(
    zcta = `zip code tabulation area`,
    income = B19013_001E,
    income_margin_of_error = B19013_001M
  ) |>
  select(zcta, income, income_margin_of_error) ->
  income_fields
```

## Convert the amounts to numbers
This changes the type of income and margin of error; the next step interprets special codes.
```{r}
#| label: convert-income-amounts
income_fields |>
  mutate(
    income = as.numeric(income),
    income_margin_of_error = as.numeric(income_margin_of_error)
  ) ->
  income_numbers
```

## Handle missing and capped estimates
Negative Census codes mean that a usable amount is unavailable. The code 250001 means “$250,000 or more,” not an exact estimate of $250,001. Record the status before replacing special values with missing values. `NA_real_` means a missing numeric value, not zero. Keep every area row.

The [Census annotation notes](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/acs-1year/data-notes.html) describe these special-value conventions.
```{r}
#| label: clean-income-special-values
income_numbers |>
  mutate(
    income_status = case_when(
      income < 0 ~ "no estimate",
      income == 250001 ~ "$250,000 or more",
      .default = "estimate"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    income = case_when(
      income_status == "estimate" ~ income,
      .default = NA_real_
    ),
    income_margin_of_error = case_when(
      income_margin_of_error < 0 ~ NA_real_,
      .default = income_margin_of_error
    )
  ) ->
  income_clean
```

## Describe relative sampling uncertainty
The coefficient of variation compares the standard error with the income estimate. Divide the supplied 90% margin of error by 1.645 to obtain the standard error, then divide by income. For ZCTA 10001, `(25244 / 1.645) / 129852` is about 11.8%. This describes sampling precision, not the accuracy of the ZIP mapping or a probability that the estimate is correct.

DECISION: Confirm the source for the 15% and 30% category boundaries. These match [Housing Assistance Council guidance](https://www.ruraldatacentral.org/Content/DataReliability), a plausible precedent rather than a verified source for this implementation. [PSRC guidance](https://psrc.github.io/psrccensus/articles/calculate-reliability-moe-transformed-acs.html) explains the calculation and similar categories. Retain the existing ordinary labels while reviewing whether lower/moderate/higher relative sampling uncertainty would be clearer. The categories are conventions, not universal divisions between trustworthy and untrustworthy data.

“Cannot calculate” means the calculation lacks an input. `income_status` still distinguishes a capped estimate from no estimate.
```{r}
#| label: describe-income-precision
income_clean |>
  mutate(income_cv = (income_margin_of_error / 1.645) / income) ->
  income_with_precision

income_with_precision |>
  mutate(
    income_reliability = case_when(
      is.na(income_cv) ~ "cannot calculate",
      income_cv < 0.15 ~ "reliable",
      income_cv < 0.30 ~ "use with care",
      .default = "unreliable"
    )
  ) ->
  area_income
```

## Prepare one ZIP-to-income lookup
For each postal ZIP, the left join attaches the income row with its assigned ZCTA. Keep all ZIPs, including any without a matching income row. Several ZIPs may share one ZCTA and its income estimate. An unmatched Census row would leave `income_status` missing; that differs from a matched row explicitly marked “no estimate.”
```{r}
#| label: prepare-zip-income
zip_areas |>
  left_join(area_income, by = "zcta") |>
  select(
    zipcode,
    zcta,
    borough,
    in_nyc,
    income,
    income_margin_of_error,
    income_status,
    income_cv,
    income_reliability
  ) ->
  zip_income
```

## Summarize the selected geography
Count postal ZIPs and distinct Census areas by the borough assigned by our rule. These counts do not claim that each area lies wholly within that borough.
```{r}
#| label: summarize-prepared-boroughs
zip_income |>
  filter(in_nyc) |>
  group_by(borough) |>
  summarise(
    zipcodes = n(),
    census_areas = n_distinct(zcta)
  )
```

## Report income availability
Count each Census area once, even when several ZIPs share it. This counts areas, not dogs.
```{r}
#| label: summarize-income-availability
zip_income |>
  filter(in_nyc) |>
  distinct(zcta, income_status) |>
  count(income_status, name = "census_areas")
```

## Inspect one mapping for each income status
Select the first ZIP in each status for display. This does not filter the prepared lookup. The supplied margin of error remains available where reported; capped or unavailable exact incomes remain missing in `income`.
```{r}
#| label: show-income-mapping-examples
zip_income |>
  filter(in_nyc) |>
  arrange(zipcode) |>
  group_by(income_status) |>
  slice_head(n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(zipcode, zcta, income, income_margin_of_error, income_status)
```
